report.tagline: An AI code editor that writes, edits and fixes code with you, now owned by SpaceX after a $60 billion deal in 2026.
report.simpleSummary: Cursor is a code editor, the app programmers type code into, with AI built in everywhere. It can finish your line, change many files at once, or run as an agent that builds a feature while you review. It looks like VS Code, the most popular editor, so switching is easy. Developers pay a monthly fee, and companies buy seats for their teams. It went from zero to over $2 billion in yearly revenue in about two years.

keyNumbers.label: Annualised revenue
keyNumbers.note: Company data shared with Reuters, via Tech Insider. It passed $1 billion in November 2025. Total including individuals may be higher.

keyNumbers.label: Acquisition price
keyNumbers.note: Announced June 2026, closed 14 August 2026, per Tech Insider. Before that it raised $2.3 billion at $29.3 billion (November 2025).

keyNumbers.note: Ramp data via CNBC. Down from 41 percent in June 2025 as Claude Code and others grew. Anthropic reportedly holds about half the category.

keyNumbers.note: a16z reported Cursor reached $100 million ARR faster than any software company, around early 2025.

keyNumbers.label: Individual plan prices
keyNumbers.note: Cursor pricing page as described by Tech Insider, November 2026: Plus $8, Premium $30, legacy Pro $20. New customers are moved to an 'X Subscription' bundle.

overview.whatItDoes: Cursor is a desktop code editor built on VS Code with AI throughout. Tab predicts your next edit, chat answers questions about your codebase, and Agent mode plans and makes multi-file changes, runs commands and fixes errors. It uses models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and now SpaceX's AI unit, plus its own Composer models.
howItWorks: Download Cursor and import your VS Code settings and extensions in one click.
Cursor indexes your codebase so the AI understands your whole project.
Tab suggests the next edit as you type; press Tab to accept.
Agent mode takes a task in plain words, edits files, runs tests and shows a diff to accept or reject.
Background agents run tasks in the cloud while you work on something else; Bugbot reviews pull requests.
Plans include a monthly amount of model usage; heavy use of top models costs extra.
overview.valueProposition: Write and change code several times faster, inside an editor that already feels familiar.

businessModel.summary: Cursor makes money from monthly subscriptions for individuals and per-seat plans for teams and enterprises, plus extra charges for heavy model use. A large part of its cost is paying model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which is why it built its own Composer models and why its pricing kept changing.

revenueStreams.detail: Plus ($8), Pro ($20, legacy) and Premium ($30) a month; new customers moved to an 'X Subscription' bundle after the SpaceX deal.
Per-user monthly pricing with admin and privacy controls; about $2.6 billion of business revenue run rate in June 2026.
Extra fees when users go beyond included model usage.
Code review add-on, $40 per user a month (legacy pricing).

businessModel.pricing: Free Hobby tier; Plus $8 a month; Pro $20 a month (legacy); Premium $30 a month; Bugbot $40 per user a month (legacy); Teams and Enterprise per seat. Pricing changed several times in 2025 to 2026.
costDrivers: Paying OpenAI, Anthropic and Google for model tokens, the largest cost
Cloud computing for indexing and background agents
businessModel.unitEconomics: A $20 a month user who asks for lots of agent work with a top model can easily use $20 to $40 of model tokens a month, so Cursor loses money on them. A light user might cost $3 to $5. This is why Cursor moved to credit-based plans in mid 2025 and why users felt the $20 plan 'ran out in a week'. Its own Composer models cost far less per task, so pushing usage to them improves margin. Rough estimates.

howTheyGetUsers: Word of mouth among developers: the product itself is the marketing

whatBringsUsersBack: The editor is where developers spend their whole workday

growth.moat: Cursor's moat is the daily habit and its usage data: billions of accepted and rejected edits train better Tab and Composer models. But switching editors is easy and rivals use the same top models, so the moat is weaker than its revenue suggests, as its falling market share shows.

pmLessons: Product-led growth works when the product gives value in minutes. Cursor grew without big sales teams.
If your main cost is a supplier who is also your rival, build your own option (Composer) early.
Pricing is part of the product. Sudden changes can undo years of goodwill.
Fast growth can hide falling market share. Track share, not only revenue.

interviewQuestions.question: Cursor's market share fell from 41 to 26 percent while revenue grew. What is happening and what would you do?
interviewQuestions.hint: Explain that the market grew faster. Find where Cursor loses (price, agents, model access). Pick one fix and a metric.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you design pricing for an AI tool where each user's cost varies a lot?
interviewQuestions.hint: Discuss flat fee versus usage-based versus credits. Protect light users, charge heavy users fairly, show a meter. Track margin and churn.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Cursor's north star metric?
interviewQuestions.hint: Accepted AI code kept by developers. Break into active developers, suggestions per developer, acceptance rate and paying users.

interviewQuestions.question: Anthropic supplies models to Cursor and also sells Claude Code. How should Cursor respond?
interviewQuestions.hint: Reduce dependence with own models, differentiate on editor experience, and offer multi-model choice. Weigh quality against cost.

interviewQuestions.question: After the SpaceX acquisition, how should Cursor reassure enterprise customers?
interviewQuestions.hint: List their worries: data, pricing, roadmap. Offer contract guarantees and clear communication. Track renewals.
